catalog_quote: In most Komo nouns, each syllable has a discrete, level tone. The following table lists the possible tones on two syllable nouns, each line representing a possible combination of tones, as indicated in the leftmost column. In the representations that follow, an acute accent indicates a high tone; the lack of an accent indicates a low tone. ... Thus, all possible combinations, or melodies, of the two tones, high and low, are attested in bisyllabic nouns. In monosyllabic nouns, however, an additional tone appears: a rising contour. ... The problem then concerns accounting for the rising tone. Here, I analyze it as being a combination of an L tone and an H tone. [p. 76] ... In the discussion so far, I have assumed that only vowels are tone-bearing units. In fact, not only vowels, but also nasals can bear tone in Komo. new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text of the UND Scholarly Commons PDF, DOI 10.31356/silwp.vol36.04; 91 form-feed pages). The running header 'SIL-UND Workpapers 1992 / page 76 / Thomas' precedes section '2 Komo lexical tone / 2.1 Nouns', and the passage reads verbatim: 'In most Komo nouns, each syllable has a discrete, level tone. The following table lists the possible tones on two syllable nouns.. In the representations that follow, an acute accent indicates a high tone; the lack of an accent indicates a low tone.. Thus, all possible combinations, or melodies, of the two tones, high and low, are attested in bisyllabic nouns. In monosyllabic nouns, however, an additional tone appears: a rising contour.' (…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Komo is a two-tone language (H vs L, with a rising contour on monosyllables) in which every syllable, and some nasals, carries a discrete lexical or grammatical tone; the tone monograph, the 1992/2011 segmental morphophonology and the 2014 dictionary phonology page never mention word stress, accent or prominence, so no stress rule is stated anywhere in the accessible descriptions.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant to stress. Tonal notes: rare high-toned nasals; word-initial nasals before voiceless obstruents get default L (whistle test, pp. 93-94).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is described at word level (nouns, verb stems) and at derivational, inflectional and post-lexical (phonological-phrase) strata; nothing on stress at any domain. The 'accent' occurrences are the acute diacritic for H tone, not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Komo/Kumu of DRC, Bantu D.23 (Guthrie), ISO kmw, glottocode komo1260, data from the Maniema/Haut-Zaire (Tshopo, Lubutu-Punia-Walikale) area; no dialect named. Not to be confused with Koman Komo of Ethiopia/Sudan (komo1258, ISO xom): Glottolog's Yehualashet 2014 'Orthography of Komo' (Lissan) belongs to komo1258 and is misfiled under this language.

sources.locator: §2.1 'Nouns', p. 76 (volume pagination; paper p. 6); also §3.4 'Digression: tone-bearing units', pp. 93-94
sources.note: Dedicated 90-page tone study: Komo has two level tones H and L (plus a rising contour on monosyllables), every syllable carries a discrete level tone, nasals can be tone-bearing, three strata of tone rules, downstep, intonation. The words 'stress' and 'accent' never occur except 'acute accent' as a tone-marking diacritic (pp. 76, 82); nothing is said about word stress or prominence.

sources.note: Segmental morphophonology (nasals, syllable structure V/CV/CVC(nasal), 7-vowel ATR and height harmony, TAM morphology, vowel copy). Zero occurrences of 'stress'/'accent'/'prominence'; no statement on word stress. Syllable-structure section 2.4 (pp. 41-42) gives no prosodic prominence rule.
